rows.question: RTI ka jawab nahi aaya to appeal kahan karni hai
queries: RTI ka jawab nahi aaya to appeal kahan karni hai
Right to Information Act appeal to first appellate authority non receipt of information
Right to Information Act section 19 appeal against decision of Central Public Information Officer
Right to Information Act second appeal to Central Information Commission or State Information Commission
topSources: The Right to Information Act, 2005 s19
The Right to Information Act, 2005 s25
The Right to Information Act, 2005 s18

rows.answer:
An appeal against not receiving a decision within the specified time can be preferred to such officer who is senior in rank to the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer in each public authority, under Section 19 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- The appeal must be preferred within thirty days from the expiry of the period specified for receiving a decision [1].
- The officer may admit the appeal after thirty days if satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing it in time [1].
- A second appeal lies with the Central Information Commission or the State Information Commission within ninety days from the date on which the decision should have been made [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 18 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 covers powers and functions of Information Commissions regarding complaints from persons who have not been given a response within the time limit [3].

rows.answer:
The punishment for identity theft is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and also a fine which may extend to rupees one lakh under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [1], and the punishment for cheating by personation by using a computer resource is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and also a fine which may extend to one lakh rupees under Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [4].

To prove the messages (electronic records) in court, any information contained in an electronic record produced by a computer or communication device shall be deemed to be a document and shall be admissible in any proceedings without further proof or production of the original, provided the conditions relating to regular computer use, proper operation, and data feed are satisfied under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 [2], which is the current law and replaced Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (previously Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872) [10].

rows.question: A company's director signed a cheque that bounced. Is the director personally liable, and can it also be cheating?
queries: A company's director signed a cheque that bounced. Is the director personally liable, and can it also be cheating?
director personal liability cheque bounce company dishonour
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 section 138
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 section 318 cheating
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s359
rows.answer:
A director who signs a cheque that bounces is personally liable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1], provided the conditions relating to presentation, notice, and failure to pay are met, and such an act can also constitute cheating under Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860) [2][10].

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier [1].
- The payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid [1].
- The drawer of the cheque must fail to make payment of the amount within fifteen days of receiving the notice [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 covers offences by companies where every person who was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business shall be deemed guilty [7].

rows.question: Is a contract signed by a 16 year old valid, and can a child be punished for a crime?
queries: Is a contract signed by a 16 year old valid, and can a child be punished for a crime?
Indian Contract Act section 11 competency of parties to contract minor agreement void
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita general exceptions age of majority child doli incapax criminal liability
topSources: The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 s14D
Binding Apprentices Act, 1850, 19 of 1850 (Rep., Act 52 of 1961) s25
rows.answer:
A contract signed by a 16-year-old is not competent under Section 11 of The Indian Contract Act, 1872, because competency requires being of the age of majority according to the law to which the person is subject [1].

A child under seven years of age cannot be punished for a crime, as nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age under Section 20 of The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 82 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [2][8].

A child above seven years and under twelve years of age can be punished for a crime only if they have attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge of the nature and consequences of their conduct on that occasion, under Section 21 of The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 83 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [3][9].

rows.answer:
The Limitation Act, 1963 shall apply to arbitrations as it applies to proceedings in court under Section 43 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1].

rows.answer: In Miranda v. Arizona, the US Supreme Court considered whether an accused must be apprised of the right not to answer and keep silent while being interrogated by the police, and observed that if a person in custody is to be subjected to interrogation, that person must first be informed in clear and unequivocal terms of the right to remain silent, which serves as a threshold requirement for an intelligent decision as to its exercise and an absolute prerequisite to overcoming the inherent pressures of the interrogation atmosphere [12]. The US Supreme Court further observed that the warning of the right to remain silent must be accompanied by the explanation that anything said can be used against the person [12].

rows.question: Shop sold me a defective phone and won't replace it, where do I complain?
queries: Shop sold me a defective phone and won't replace it, where do I complain?
defective goods replacement refund consumer complaint jurisdiction
Consumer Protection Act 2019 section 34 district commission jurisdiction
Consumer Protection Act 2019 section 35 manner in which complaint shall be made
rows.answer:
The District Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees, as provided under Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- The complaint may be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the opposite party resides, carries on business, has a branch office, or personally works for gain, or where the cause of action arises, or where the complainant resides or personally works for gain, according to Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 [1].
- The complaint may be filed by the consumer to whom the goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered, under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 [2].

Related provisions:
- Section 101 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provides the power of the Central Government to make rules, including those relating to the fee and manner of filing complaints under Section 35 [7].

The High Court has the power to issue writs including habeas corpus for the enforcement of rights and any other purpose under Article 226 of the Constitution of India [2].

Conditions and time limits:
- The High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises may exercise the power to issue directions, orders or writs, notwithstanding that the seat of the Government or authority or the residence of the person is not within those territories under Article 226 of the Constitution of India [2].
- Where an interim order is made against any party on a petition under clause (1) of Article 226 without furnishing copies of the petition and documents or without giving an opportunity of being heard, and that party applies to the High Court to vacate it, the High Court shall dispose of the application within two weeks from the date of receipt or the date of furnishing the copy (or by the next open day if closed), and if not disposed of, the interim order shall stand vacated under Article 226 of the Constitution of India [2].

rows.question: notice period for cheque bounce
queries: notice period for cheque bounce
dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds notice period demand
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 notice within thirty days
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 cause of action payment within fifteen days
rows.answer:
The notice for payment must be given in writing within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee or holder in due course from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier [1].
- The payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within 30 days of receiving information from the bank that the cheque was returned unpaid [1].
- The drawer must fail to make the payment within 15 days of receiving the said notice [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 covers cognizance of offences, stating that no court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 except upon a complaint in writing made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises [8].
- Section 7 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 covers the dishonour of electronic funds transfer for insufficiency of funds, apply
